findings.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:121 — [P1][100] Per-group authorization resources are created without the resource-type discriminator that the new membership-discovery path owns as its data-model key. Anchor: `getOrCreateResource`. Code: `resource = resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId());`. Concrete failure: a permission created for one group produces a resource with no `Groups` type, so `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`'s `findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` never enumerates it and user searches/counts supplied by that method omit every member of individually permitted groups. Strongest rebuttal: scope permission creation may infer the type from its request; it fails because this method creates and persists the Resource itself and never calls `setType(resourceType)`, while the prior Group implementation explicitly sets its resource type.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — [P1][100] Membership discovery crosses the resource/domain-ID boundary using the authorization resource UUID where the evaluator and user provider require the GroupModel ID. Anchor: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`. Code: `if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)) { granted.add(groupResource.getId()); }`. Concrete failure: for any enumerated per-group resource, `hasPermission` calls `findByName(server, groupId)` with its resource UUID rather than its name (the group ID), falls back to the all-groups resource or returns false, and the returned set contains no usable group IDs; filtered user search/count endpoints therefore return zero members for an individually granted group. Strongest rebuttal: resource and group IDs might be intended to coincide; it fails because the schema creates the resource with `create(..., name, ...)`, making the group ID its name, while the authorization store assigns a distinct resource ID.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — [P1][100] The global group management guard conflates read and write scopes, violating the scope ownership contract. Anchor: `canManage`. Code: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`. Concrete failure: a principal granted only the all-groups `view` scope satisfies `requireManage()` and can create groups through `GroupsResource`, despite holding no `manage` scope. Strongest rebuttal: `view` might deliberately imply management for all groups; it fails because the same class's per-group `canManage(GroupModel)` accepts only `MANAGE`, and the schema exposes `VIEW` and `MANAGE` as distinct scopes.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — [100][P1] `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` makes an all-groups `view` grant satisfy `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()`'s `requireManage()`, so a view-only administrator can create groups.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — [100][P1] `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)` and `granted.add(groupResource.getId());` use the authorization-resource UUID where the user-provider expects the Keycloak group ID, so scoped member-view permissions do not constrain user search/count pagination to the authorized groups and the user-count endpoint returns zero for those grants.

server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:250 — [100] P1 migration safety: `if (client != null) { return; }` makes the schema expansion apply only to newly enabled realms, so an existing persisted V2 realm retains no `Groups` all-resource or `manage-membership`/`manage-members`/`view-members` scopes; creating its first Groups scope permission fails scope lookup rather than enabling the feature after upgrade.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — [100] P1 anchor: `canManage()`; code: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`; a principal granted only the new all-groups `view` scope now passes `requireManage()` and can create or otherwise globally manage groups, instead of receiving Forbidden; strongest rebuttal: the method could intentionally treat viewing as management, but that fails because `canManage(GroupModel)` at line 79 accepts only `MANAGE` and the schema defines `VIEW` and `MANAGE` as distinct scopes, so this silently collapses the requested scope boundary.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — [100] [P1] [anchor:getGroupIdsWithViewPermission] code: `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)` — A per-group `VIEW_MEMBERS`/`MANAGE_MEMBERS` grant silently produces an empty group-ID set: `hasPermission` looks that value up with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141), but this code passes the authorization resource ID rather than its name (the underlying Keycloak group ID). Consequently `/users` and `/users/count` return HTTP 200 with zero matching members for every individually granted group. Rebuttal: all-groups policies mask this by taking the fallback path; survival: normal per-group policies always retain distinct resource IDs and names.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:121 — [75] [P2] [anchor:getGroupIdsWithViewPermission] code: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(...)) ... })` — Every restricted-admin `/users` search or count traverses every `Groups` authorization resource and evaluates policy once per resource, with no bound, pagination, or cache. As the realm reaches N group resources, one request deterministically executes N authorization evaluations and eventually exceeds its request/database time budget, returning a timeout/5xx instead of a bounded response. Rebuttal: admins with global user view short-circuit; survival: the restricted-admin path is exactly the one that needs per-group member visibility.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — [100] P1 improper authorization: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` makes an administrator granted only the all-groups `VIEW` scope pass `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup`'s `requireManage()` gate and create arbitrary realm groups (or move an existing child to the top level); the strongest rebuttal is that per-group management still requires `MANAGE`, but it fails because this global mutating endpoint invokes the no-argument evaluator.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:254 — [75] [P2] The only group-list assertion uses `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).groups().groups()` (the default `populateHierarchy=true`), so it never reaches the changed flat-list branch `return stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` in `GroupsResource`; if that filter is removed or evaluates the wrong permission, `GET /groups?populateHierarchy=false` returns groups outside the caller's grant while this test still passes. Add the same deny/one-granted-group assertions with `populateHierarchy=false` (and a search/q request, which also uses that branch).

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:129 — [75] [P2] `testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers` proves `MANAGE_MEMBERS` through `users().search(...)` and `update(...)`, but it does not exercise the newly extended `canMapRoles` or `canManageGroupMembership` paths: `return hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user);`. A regression that omits `canManageByGroup(user)` from either branch leaves member-user updates green but rejects role mapping or group membership changes for the same MANAGE_MEMBERS grant. Exercise both operations after granting only `MANAGE_MEMBERS`, with a distinct target group/user and a real role.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:103 — [75] [P2] The group-member visibility tests only call `users().search(...)`; they do not execute the changed brute-force lookup setup `Set<String> groupIds = auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission();` in `BruteForceUsersResource`. If that endpoint fails to install the group-ID session attribute (or regresses to the former condition), the brute-force user list omits every user visible solely through `VIEW_MEMBERS`/`MANAGE_MEMBERS` while all added tests pass. Add an endpoint-level assertion for the brute-force search with a group-scoped member grant.

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at AdminPermissionsSchema.java lines 86-121 in the diff, the getOrCreateResource method creates a new Resource at line 121 with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` but never calls `setType(resourceType)` on the created resource. The method receives `resourceType` as a parameter (line 86) and uses it in the switch statement to resolve the name (lines 107-111), but the actual Resource creation doesn't set the type. If resources are created without the type being set, findByType won't find them, causing the membership discovery to fail. This is a real bug where the resource type is not being set on newly created resources.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in GroupPermissionsV2.java lines 115-125, the method iterates over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and calls `groupResource.getId()`. In AdminPermissionsSchema, when creating resources via getOrCreateResource(), for groups it calls resolveGroup() which returns `group.getId()` (the Keycloak group ID), not a separate authorization resource UUID. The resource name/id is set to the group's actual ID. So `groupResource.getId()` returns the group ID that was used to create/name the resource, which is the Keycloak group ID. The diff shows additions of GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, new scopes (MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP, MANAGE_MEMBERS, VIEW_MEMBERS), and a resolveGroup method, but no conditional logic about 'client != null' that would affect schema expansion or migration. adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java lines 65-72, the canManage() method returns true if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) returns true. This means a user with only VIEW scope on all-groups would pass canManage() check. However, canManage(GroupModel) at lines 75-82 only accepts MANAGE scope (not VIEW). This inconsistency means global canManage() is more permissive than per-group canManage(). The requireManage() method in parent class GroupPermissions calls canManage() (the global one), so a user with only VIEW permission could pass requireManage() and potentially create groups or perform other management operations. This appears to be a real bug where VIEW scope incorrectly grants management capabilities at the global level.

Rebuttal: all-groups policies mask this by taking the fallback path; survival: normal per-group policies always retain distinct resource IDs and names.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` passes the wrong ID. However, looking at the code in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` at line 122, it iterates over resources of type `GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE` and calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`. The `hasPermission` method at line 141 does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` where `groupId` is the parameter passed. Looking at `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()`, when creating group resources, the name is set to `resolveGroup()` which returns `group.getId()` - meaning the resource name IS the group ID. So when `groupResource.getId()` is passed (which is the resource's own ID, not the group ID), this would indeed be different from the resource name. However, the finding misunderstands the flow - when `hasPermission` is called with a groupId, if `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` returns null, it falls back to the type-level resource. The actual issue is that `groupResource.getId()` returns the authorization resource ID, but the code should be passing the group ID (which is stored as the resource name). But examining `resolveGroup()`, it returns `group.getId()` as the name, so resources are named by group ID. The finding's analysis appears incorrect about the actual behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real performance concern in the new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() method at line 121. The code iterates through all group resources via resourceStore.findByType() and calls hasPermission() for each one, which involves policy evaluation. This is unbounded - as the number of groups grows, this becomes O(N) authorization evaluations per request. While this is a valid architectural/scalability concern introduced by the diff, it's not strictly a bug (the code is functionally correct) but rather a performance design issue that could cause problems at scale. The finding correctly notes that admins with global view permission short-circuit early, but restricted admins hit this path.

Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (lines 68-74), it returns true if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) - meaning VIEW scope is sufficient to pass canManage(). adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. Looking at GroupsResource.java in the diff, there are two code paths: one with `populateHierarchy=true` (line 110-111) and one with `populateHierarchy=false` (line 113-114) which uses `stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)`. The test file GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java only calls `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).groups().groups()` without specifying `populateHierarchy=false`, meaning it only tests the hierarchy path. The new permission filtering logic in the flat-list branch (`stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)`) is not exercised by these tests. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added permission logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:129 — [75] [P2] `testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers` proves `MANAGE_MEMBERS` through `users().search(...)` and `update(...)`, but it does not exercise the newly extended `canMapRoles` or `canManageGroupMembership` paths: `return hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user);`. A regression that omits `canManageByGroup(user)` from either branch leaves member-user updates green but rejects role mapping or group membership changes for the same MANAGE_MEMBERS grant. Exercise both operations after granting only `MANAGE_MEMBERS`, with a distinct target group/user and a real role.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers only tests search() and update() operations after granting MANAGE_MEMBERS permission, but doesn't test the canMapRoles or canManageGroupMembership paths that were modified in UserPermissionsV2.java to include '|| canManageByGroup(user)'. The diff shows these methods now have the pattern 'hasPermission(...) || canManageByGroup(user)', and canManageByGroup delegates to groups().canManageMembers(). A test that only verifies update() doesn't ensure the role mapping or group membership management paths work correctly with MANAGE_MEMBERS permission. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:103 — [75] [P2] The group-member visibility tests only call `users().search(...)`; they do not execute the changed brute-force lookup setup `Set<String> groupIds = auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission();` in `BruteForceUsersResource`. If that endpoint fails to install the group-ID session attribute (or regresses to the former condition), the brute-force user list omits every user visible solely through `VIEW_MEMBERS`/`MANAGE_MEMBERS` while all added tests pass. Add an endpoint-level assertion for the brute-force search with a group-scoped member grant.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new test file GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java tests user visibility through group membership permissions using `users().search()` calls, but does not test the BruteForceUsersResource endpoint which has its own modified code path for `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`. The diff shows BruteForceUsersResource.java was modified to use the new `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` method, but the test file only tests the regular UsersResource path. This is a valid test coverage gap - if the brute-force endpoint regresses, these tests would not catch it. However, this is a missing test scenario rather than a bug in the code itself.
